name: Muscle dysmorphia (bigorexia)

card.summary: A body-image condition where people feel too small despite being muscular; recognised in psychiatry, discussed in lifting and looksmaxxing circles as 'bigorexia'.
card.note: A clinical condition, not a technique; treatment research is limited mostly to case reports.

quick.overview:
Muscle dysmorphia is a subtype of body dysmorphic disorder in which a person believes their body is too small or not muscular enough, even when they are already muscular. It is often called bigorexia or reverse anorexia, and is reported more among gym members, bodybuilders and anabolic steroid users.

In looksmaxxing and fitness communities the term comes up in discussions of size, leanness and perceived smallness. Researchers describe it as a recognised clinical condition rather than a lifestyle approach.
quick.mechanism: Clinicians describe a distorted perception of one's own muscularity driving compulsive training, dietary rules, overtraining and sometimes use of performance-enhancing drugs. Reported risk factors include steroid use, trauma, bullying, perfectionism, low self-esteem and exposure to idealised muscular bodies.
quick.risks: Reported consequences include co-occurring eating, mood, anxiety and substance use disorders, social avoidance, injury from overtraining, and in adolescents a proposed cardiovascular strain. Treatment research is limited, mostly case reports; family-based therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy and SSRIs have some supporting evidence according to Wikipedia's summary.

lead: Muscle dysmorphia, popularly called bigorexia, megarexia or reverse anorexia, is a subtype of body dysmorphic disorder in which a person believes their body is too small or not muscular enough, often despite being large and well trained [1]. It sits at the centre of a tension in physique-building: the same drive that produces training consistency, careful eating and attention to detail can, in some people, stop tracking how the body actually looks. For anyone working on their physique, knowing the pattern is a way to keep the pursuit of muscle tied to the body in the mirror rather than to a persistent sense of smallness.

The DSM-5 (2013) classifies it as a specifier under body dysmorphic disorder, and ICD-11 lists it as a subtype [1][20]. Some researchers have argued it fits better as an eating disorder, because affected people show rigid diets and high scores on eating-attitude measures, or as a behavioural addiction, because exercise and dietary routines can become compulsive [1]. Estimates of how common it is range from about 1% to 54% of men depending on the group studied, with higher rates reported among gym members, weightlifters, bodybuilders and anabolic steroid users [1].

The concept was developed in the 1990s by Harrison Pope and colleagues, who first described a pattern they called reverse anorexia in male bodybuilders and later argued it was a form of body dysmorphic disorder [1][9]. Since then the research literature has grown quickly, with a 2016 count cited by Wikipedia putting half of all peer-reviewed articles on the topic in the preceding five years [1]. Recent reviews focus on adolescents and young men, the role of social media, steroid use and prevention programmes [7][8][13].

The term bigorexia also circulates well outside the clinic. Gym communities, fitness forums and looksmaxxing spaces use it to talk about feeling small, bulking and cutting cycles and comparison with edited physiques, and press coverage of social media and photo filters has helped spread it [18][21][22][23].

paras: The defining feature is a belief that one's body is too small or insufficiently muscular [1]. Clinical descriptions include excessive muscle-building effort, rigid diets or dietary restriction, overtraining, use of growth-enhancing drugs, spending more than three hours a day thinking about muscularity, wearing layers of clothing to look bigger, checking the body closely, and avoiding places or people that might expose the perceived deficiency [1]. About half of affected people have poor or no insight that their perception is unrealistic [1].

Onset is usually in the late teens or early twenties, although body dissatisfaction has been found in boys as young as six [1]. Work and school absences and social impairment are reported [1]. Muscularity dissatisfaction has been reported to affect quality of life more than dissatisfaction with body fat or height in men who have sex with men [1]. Researchers separate several facets of body-image disturbance (evaluative, perceptual, cognitive-affective and behavioural); a systematic review of 167 controlled studies found the largest gaps from control groups in body dissatisfaction, and noted few studies with male and muscle dysmorphia clinical samples [10].

Co-occurring eating, mood, anxiety and substance use disorders are reported, and suicide attempt rates are described as high compared with other forms of body dysmorphic disorder [1]. Muscle dysmorphia and disordered eating are reported to correlate more with each other than either does with body dysmorphic disorder in general [1].

Body dysmorphic disorder itself has a longer history. The Italian physician Enrico Morselli described dysmorphophobia in the 1880s; the American Psychiatric Association added it to DSM-III in 1980 and renamed it body dysmorphic disorder in 1987 [20].

Pope, Katz and Hudson studied 108 male bodybuilders in 1993 and described reverse anorexia, an inversion of anorexia nervosa in which the drive is to be bigger rather than thinner [1]. In 1997 Pope and colleagues published a paper describing muscle dysmorphia as an underrecognised form of body dysmorphic disorder [1][9]. Pope, Phillips and Olivardia's 2000 book The Adonis Complex brought the topic to a general readership as a book about male body obsession [1]. A 2009 paper in European Eating Disorders Review discussed it under the heading bigorexia in a bodybuilding context [11]. DSM-5 (2013) placed it under body dysmorphic disorder with a muscularity specifier [1][20]. The 2005 Journal of Athletic Training review set out recognition and referral options for athletic trainers [2].

Reported risk factors include anabolic steroid use, trauma such as sexual assault, domestic violence or bullying about smallness or weakness, low self-esteem, vulnerable narcissism, perfectionism, involvement in sports where size or weight gives an edge, and, among gay and bisexual men, minority stress and internalised heterosexism [1]. Wikipedia notes that internalising idealised muscular male bodies in media is a strong predictor of muscularity pursuit among college-aged men and that fitness magazines and advertising have featured increasingly muscular male bodies since the 1980s [1].

A systematic review of anabolic-androgenic steroid use in athletes reports that motivations are mainly performance and body-image improvement, that users often present with somatoform and eating disorders, and that it is unclear whether steroids cause conditions such as muscle dysmorphia or whether people with these conditions are drawn to steroids [13]. A systematic review of 22 mostly cross-sectional studies (five on muscle dysmorphia) found that higher social media use was generally associated with more symptoms [8]. A 2026 study used machine learning to look at gendered stereotypes and body-image concerns on diet and fitness forums [6].

Prevalence depends on sample and instrument and ranges from about 1% to 54% of men in different studied groups [1]. It is rarer in women but occurs, for example in female bodybuilders with a history of sexual assault [1]. Cases have been identified in China, South Africa and Latin America, while a Taiwanese study found lower rates in a population less exposed to Western media [1]. A review of male eating disorders notes that muscularity-focused concerns and sexual orientation increase risk in adolescent males [12], and a review of eating disorders in male athletes covers related concerns in sport [26].
In a sample of 384 male bodybuilders, 5.7% reported muscle dysmorphia, and younger age and protein powder use were associated with higher scores [3].

Disordered eating in this group often runs toward rigid, high-protein plans rather than restriction for thinness. A Spanish study of 141 male gym users aged 18 to 45 who wanted to increase muscle mass analysed their body mass index and 24-hour diet and assessed muscle dysmorphia with the Muscle Appearance Satisfaction Scale [4].

In a within-subjects crossover study of 30 regularly training young men (mean age about 21), participants completed the Muscle Dysmorphic Disorder Inventory in different conditions around a weight training session, examining how symptoms vary with training [14]. A 2026 review has proposed that bigorexia-related behaviours may be linked to early cardiovascular injury in adolescents [5].

Research on treatment is limited, mainly case reports and clinical experience, and no protocol has been validated [1]. Family-based therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy and SSRIs have some supporting evidence, and eating disorder treatments may also help [1]. For body dysmorphic disorder generally, SSRIs and CBT, including a BDD-specific CBT manual with exposure and response prevention, are described as effective, and cosmetic surgery usually does not relieve distress [20]. Lack of insight and avoidance of care are described as obstacles to treatment [1].

The 2026 Lancet Child & Adolescent Health review reports that some approaches show promise but outcome data in large, diverse clinical adolescent samples remain scarce, that muscle dysmorphia-specific prevention strategies are few, and that future research should examine pharmacotherapy, prevention and cross-cultural assessment [7].

Observational and cross-sectional studies dominate. A study of 384 male bodybuilders linked higher muscle dysmorphia scores to younger age, protein powder use and social physique anxiety [3], and a Spanish gym-user study examined diets in men screened for the condition [4]. A systematic review pooled mostly cross-sectional work on social media [8].

Randomised work has centred on prevention. The Body Project: More Than Muscles, a dissonance-based programme for men with body dissatisfaction, was tested in a 2017 randomised trial [15]. Further randomised trials covered Brazilian men (an in-person programme after online training, 2021, and a 1-year follow-up in 2024), Brazilian gay and bisexual men with a 1-year follow-up, and a 2026 trial comparing a virtual peer-led programme to media advocacy in young adult men with body-image concerns [16][17][24][25]. The Lancet review states that eating disorder prevention programmes show potential for reducing muscle dysmorphia symptoms [7]. No randomised trial of a treatment specific to diagnosed muscle dysmorphia is listed in these sources.

In gym and appearance communities the word bigorexia is used loosely for feeling small, endless bulking and comparison with other lifters. Wikipedia describes looksmaxxing as ranging from skincare and gym use to extreme dieting and unauthorised substance use, including anabolic steroids, and cites BBC, Guardian and Conversation coverage in 2024 saying communities that rate people's looks can contribute to body dysmorphia [19].

Press stories have helped the term circulate. Hacker News discussions link to coverage under headlines such as one in ten men in gyms believed to have bigorexia (2015), the rise of muscle dysmorphia (2019), social media spurring muscle dysmorphia in teenage boys (2022) and an association between photo-filter use and muscle dysmorphia (2024) [18][21][22][23]. Wikipedia's article on body dysmorphic disorder notes that plastic surgeon Tijon Esho coined the term Snapchat dysmorphia in 2018 for patients seeking to resemble filtered photos [20].

Muscle dysmorphia overlaps with other conditions in the literature: eating disorders, exercise dependence, orthorexia nervosa, and anabolic-androgenic steroid use and dependence [8][13]. Wikipedia describes it as an inverse counterpart of anorexia nervosa in the earliest conceptualisation [1].

lore.intro: In gym, bodybuilding and looksmaxxing conversation, bigorexia is used both as a clinical term and as shorthand for feeling permanently small; media stories about social media and filtered physiques feed the discussion [18][21][22][23].

claims.claim: Bigorexia is just an extreme version of normal gym dedication
claims.believers: The claim is that constant bulking, rigid meal plans and daily training are ordinary commitment to a goal.
claims.experts: Clinicians describe the condition by distress, impairment, hours a day spent on muscularity, concealment and avoidance, not by training volume alone; roughly half of affected people lack insight [1][2].

claims.claim: Social media and edited physiques make men feel smaller
claims.believers: Users and commentators say constant exposure to lean, muscular, filtered bodies drives comparison and a feeling of being too small [21][22].
claims.experts: A systematic review of 22 mostly cross-sectional studies found higher social media use generally associated with more muscle dysmorphia and orthorexia symptoms, in mostly non-clinical samples [8].

claims.believers: The claim is that chasing size with steroids leaves users never feeling big enough.
claims.experts: A systematic review says it is unclear whether steroids cause muscle dysmorphia or whether people with it are drawn to steroids, and notes that users often present with somatoform and eating disorders [13].

claims.claim: Looksmaxxing and rating communities can feed body dysmorphia
claims.believers: Critics quoted in the press say communities that score faces and bodies encourage fixation on perceived flaws.
claims.experts: Wikipedia cites BBC, Guardian and Conversation coverage from 2024 making this argument; no controlled study of looksmaxxing communities and muscle dysmorphia is cited [19].

claims.claim: Muscle dysmorphia is treatable like other body dysmorphic conditions
claims.believers: The claim is that approaches used for other body dysmorphic conditions, such as therapy and SSRIs, carry over to muscle dysmorphia.
claims.experts: Family-based therapy, CBT and SSRIs have some supporting evidence, but research on this subtype is mostly case reports and no protocol is validated [1]; prevention programmes show promise in randomised trials [7][15].

claims.claim: Only teenage boys and bodybuilders are affected
claims.believers: The popular image is of competitive bodybuilders or adolescents on social media.
claims.experts: Prevalence estimates range from 1% to 54% of men across groups; cases are reported in women, in gay and bisexual men and in several countries [1].

claims.claim: Bigorexia affects the heart through extreme training and enhancement
claims.believers: The claim is that extreme bulking, restrictive routines and drug use may strain the cardiovascular system in young people.
claims.experts: A 2026 review proposes a cardiovascular framework in adolescents with bigorexia-related behaviours; it is a conceptual proposal rather than a trial result [5].

chain: Persistent belief that the body is too small
Compulsive training, rigid eating, steroid or supplement use
Recognising the pattern allows earlier support and a physique goal that is not driven by distortion
angle.text: The condition is relevant to people pursuing size because it describes when muscle-building becomes driven by a perception of smallness rather than the actual physique. Clinicians use awareness of its signs, such as hours a day spent on muscularity, concealing the body, or rigid training and diet, to guide referral and support.
